findings.title: Blocklist lookup is case-sensitive, so changing the case of an address bypasses it
findings.body: should_block? does BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first with no normalization, and EmailValidator passes the raw submitted value. A blocked entry 'bad@spamclub.com' does not match 'Bad@spamclub.com', and the unique index on blocked_emails.email is also case-sensitive, so rows differing only by case can coexist and .first picks one arbitrarily. Anyone blocked can register again by changing the case of any letter. The codebase already has Email.downcase (used in users_controller#change_email and User.find_by_username_or_email), so both the stored value and the lookup should be normalized the same way.

findings.title: Validation side effect increments match_count on every valid? call, so one signup counts twice
findings.body: should_block? writes to the database (match_count += 1, last_match_at, save) and it runs inside the User email validator. Every valid? call counts as a match. UsersController#create calls user.valid? (line 168) and then user.save (line 172), which runs validations again, so one blocked signup attempt increments match_count by 2 and the statistics the spec describes as 'whether those emails have ever been blocked' are inflated. Any other valid? call, such as a form or preview check, also counts. The counter should be incremented once per blocked attempt (for example in the controller or a dedicated check), not as a side effect of validation.

findings.title: match_count is updated with a non-atomic read-modify-write
findings.body: record.match_count += 1 followed by record.save reads the current value and writes back the incremented one. Two concurrent signups for the same blocked address can both read N and both write N+1, losing an increment. Use an atomic update (for example BlockedEmail.update_counters(record.id, match_count: 1) or a SQL increment) together with the last_match_at update.

findings.title: Domain whitelist/blacklist regex is unanchored, so it matches addresses where the domain is only a substring
findings.body: Regexp.new("@(#{domains})", true) matches the domain anywhere after an '@'. With a whitelist containing gmail.com, an address like x@gmail.com.attacker.net satisfies the check and passes, which defeats the whitelist. With a blacklist containing spamclub.com, a@spamclub.com.example.org is also rejected. This logic was moved here verbatim from User, but this PR rewrites it into a new validator and it is a security control, so the pattern should be anchored to the end of the address (for example matching '@domain' followed by end of string, case-insensitively).

findings.title: Any server email error marks the address as rejected and then shows a generic 'is invalid' reason
findings.body: The new branch adds result.values.email to rejectedEmails for any result.errors.email, including 'has already been taken' and 'is not allowed from that email provider'. emailValidation then returns the fixed reason I18n 'user.email.invalid' (lines 69-73) for that address, so the field says 'is invalid' even when the address is valid and was rejected for another reason. The flash message shows the server reason, but the field and the form state contradict it, which is misleading to the user.

findings.title: Validator spec stubs the blocklist, so no test exercises the real blocking path or the moved domain rules
findings.body: Both examples stub BlockedEmail.should_block?, so the table, the case-sensitivity behavior, and the match_count side effect are never exercised here. Nothing verifies that a User with a blocked address fails validation, that a case variant is blocked, or that the whitelist/blacklist branches, which this file now owns, still behave as before. The double-counting issue would also go unnoticed. Add a spec that creates a BlockedEmail record and checks User validity end to end, including a case variant and a count-after-valid? expectation.
